crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Drafting a Manuscript
children.blurb: Drafting a manuscript is the stage of academic writing where a researcher turns results, methods and reasoning into a document that a journal or conference can review.

children.name: Testing Arguments Before Peer Review
children.blurb: Testing arguments before peer review is the practice of checking a paper's reasoning, evidence and internal consistency while the manuscript is still in the author's hands, rather than waiting for referees to find the gaps.

children.name: Disciplinary Register and Language
children.blurb: Disciplinary register and language covers the conventions of vocabulary, tone, hedging and structure that mark a text as belonging to a particular field.

children.name: Plagiarism and AI Detection
children.blurb: Plagiarism and AI detection covers the tools and practices used to judge whether a piece of writing was copied from an existing source or produced by a generative model.

children.name: Explaining Research After Publication
children.blurb: Explaining research after publication covers the work of translating a finished paper for readers who will not read the paper itself: press releases, plain language summaries, blog posts, thread write ups, and talks.

sections.body: Academic writing and peer review is the part of research life where a draft becomes a claim other people can check, and language models now sit inside that work at several points. They help researchers turn notes into a readable manuscript, restate an argument in different words to see whether it still holds, and adjust a paper toward the register of a specific field. They also get used to screen text for overlap with published work and to explain finished research to readers outside the specialty. The work is textual and argumentative rather than experimental, so the tools are doing drafting, reformulation and comparison, not discovery. What they produce is a draft or a signal that a person then has to judge.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Drafting and register adjustment are the most settled uses, because a model can imitate the shape of a methods section or a humanities abstract and a writer can edit the result. Testing arguments is harder, since a model can generate counterarguments but cannot tell whether they matter to the field. Plagiarism and AI detection is the least reliable area: detectors produce false positives on ordinary academic prose and on writing by non-native speakers, and no detector output is treated as proof on its own. The honest limits run through all of it. A model does not know the literature, cannot verify a citation it has not seen, and will state a fabricated reference with the same confidence as a real one. Originality and authorship are judged by editors, committees and readers, not by software scores.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages follow the life of a paper from first draft to public explanation. Drafting a Manuscript is the starting point, for turning raw material into a structured text a journal could receive. Testing Arguments Before Peer Review takes that draft and stress tests the reasoning, which is where a model is useful as a sparring partner rather than a writer. Disciplinary Register and Language covers the tone and vocabulary conventions that make a paper sound like it belongs in its field, and it is the page to read when a draft is correct but reads as foreign to the discipline. Plagiarism and AI Detection deals with the checks applied to a manuscript and the serious limits of those checks, and a reader should go there before trusting any similarity or AI score. Explaining Research After Publication is the far end, where the work is translated for readers beyond the specialty and the same tools are used for a different audience and a different purpose.
